extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners and patent practitioners evaluating subject-matter eligibility (Section 101) for business-method and related claims
extracted.subtask_description: Apply the Alice/Mayo two-step framework to determine whether patent claims (here, business-method and computer-implemented claims) are directed to a judicial exception and, if so, whether additional elements individually or in combination supply an 'inventive concept' (significantly more).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — statutory category
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim recites a statutory category of invention (e.g., process, machine, manufacture, composition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example language: 'The claim recites a method ... Thus, the claim is directed to a process, which is a statutory category of invention (Step 1: Yes).' If the claim falls into a statutory category, proceed to analyze judicial exceptions (Step 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A — directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze whether the claim is 'directed to' a judicial exception, such as an abstract idea (e.g., fundamental economic practices or long-prevalent business practices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the recited steps that describe the purported abstract idea by pointing to the language of the claim (e.g., 'fraud prevention by identity verification' or 'inventory management'). Explain similarity to concepts courts previously found abstract (examples: intermediated settlement, risk hedging, mental processes). The guidance notes that fraud prevention by verifying identity is a 'long prevalent' business practice and is similar to claims found abstract in cases like CyberSource.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — inventive concept / 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: If claim is directed to an abstract idea, analyze whether any additional element or combination of elements ensures the claim amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception (i.e., supplies an inventive concept).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both individual additional elements and their combination. The analysis should ask whether elements merely recite conventional or generic technology or whether they provide a non-conventional and non-generic implementation that improves the relevant technical field. Use precedent distinctions (e.g., Diehr and Bascom show combinations can supply significantly more when they effect a technical improvement; mere automation of a business practice does not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional or generic computer components do not supply inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements that merely recite generic computer components (e.g., a processor, memory, mobile device) performing conventional or routine functions do not, by themselves, provide significantly more than an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the text: 'a processor comparing data' and 'a memory and processor configured to perform steps' were described as 'well-understood, routine, conventional generic functions' and therefore insufficient. Similarly, reading data, generating random codes, and analyzing data at a high level of generality are treated as conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant pre-solution activity / mere data gathering is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: High-level data-gathering steps or pre-solution activity recited at a general level are considered insignificant and do not make a claim patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidance treats obtaining customer-specific information from a bank card as an example of data gathering that, when recited at a high level, 'amounts to insignificant pre-solution activity' or 'mere data gathering' necessary to use the abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination can supply inventive concept if non-conventional, non-generic, and addresses unique technical problems
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination of otherwise conventional elements may nonetheless amount to significantly more if the combination operates in a non-conventional and non-generic way that provides a practical implementation improving a technical field or addressing unique problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text example: Claim 2's combination (ATM provides random code, mobile device generates encrypted image in response, ATM decrypts and analyzes image, then controls keypad access) 'operates in a non-conventional and non-generic way' to verify identity more securely; thus the combination presented a 'specific, discrete implementation' and provided an inventive concept. Compare to Bascom and DDR where unconventional sequencing or specific architectures mattered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner rejection content guidance (what a rejection should explain)
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting under Section 101, clearly identify the abstract idea and explain why the claim's additional limitations are conventional or merely generic computer components performing generic functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance text: 'A rejection of claim 1 should identify the abstract idea by pointing to the language of the claim ... and explain that fraud-prevention by identity verification is similar to concepts that courts have previously found abstract. The rejection should identify the additional limitations ... and explain why those limitations are conventional or are only generic computer components performing generic functions and are mere automation of economic business practices.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner allowance / eligibility explanation guidance (what helps show eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although an examiner need not always provide an extensive explanation of eligibility, the record is enhanced when the examiner gives clarifying remarks pointing to the reason for eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: For an eligible claim, 'clarification could easily be made by simply pointing to the combination of elements used in the non-conventional implementation of identity verification.' Providing such rationale in the record helps explain why the claim amounts to significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use relevant case law precedent comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the claim under review to relevant Federal Circuit and Supreme Court decisions to determine whether the patent eligibility result should follow precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidance repeatedly compares claims to precedents (e.g., CyberSource, Diehr, Bascom, Enfish, Electric Power Group, Content Extraction, TLI Communications, Digitech, DDR) to explain why a claim is or is not an abstract idea or why it does or does not contain an inventive concept. Use similarities/differences in claimed features and technical improvements as the basis for comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting or manipulating particular information alone does not avoid abstractness
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting that the claim selects, collects, stores, or manipulates particular information (image data, classification data, location data) does not by itself render the claim non-abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text states: 'the mere selection and manipulation of particular information by itself does not make an abstract concept any less abstract.' Cites Electric Power Group and Digitech as examples where mere information manipulation remained abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the claim 'as a whole' — both individual elements and their combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether individual additional elements and their combination, when viewed together in the context of the entire claim, provide significantly more than the abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidance emphasizes examining elements taken individually and in combination. For example, even if individual elements are conventional, their specific combination may supply an inventive concept (or may not). The analysis should explain why viewing the limitations in combination either fails or succeeds to provide significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting for eligibility: recite specific technical improvements, not high-level functions
rubrics_metrics.description: To increase the likelihood of eligibility, claims should recite concrete technical solutions and specific limitations (e.g., particular hardware arrangements, algorithms, data structures, ordered sequences) rather than high-level, generic computer functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventory example: claims reciting a 'high-resolution video camera array' with 'overlapping views', contour+character recognition, supervised training and 3-D reconstruction were found to recite specific technical improvements (in claims 2 and 3) and thus could amount to significantly more. Contrast with claims that merely recite storing images and classification data using a generic processor and memory, which were treated as abstract.
